These Númenórean gloves grant their wearer relentless stamina and courage.
This helm was named not for its colour, but for the dream the wearer had of returning to Khazad-dûm and recovering the Moria-silver found there.
The wearer of this Númenórean helm knows little weariness.
This helm was worn by a man of Bree-land during the wars with Angmar long ago.
This helm somehow survived the fall of Beleriand and was at last washed ashore on the coast of Middle-earth.
This helm was crafted in the peaceful glades of Lothlórien in ages past.
These leggings were tailored by the Eglain of the Lone-lands to guard against snake-bites.
These Númenórean leggings grant the wearer protection against many kinds of attacks.
These leggings are rumoured to have been crafted from leather taken from the Kine of Araw, but that is only legend.
Edstan, an archer from Dale, always believed this rock gave him great luck.
These leggings from Lothlórien grant their wearer greatly renewed endurance.
This beryl was carried by the Elf Mellonor of Mirkwood, whose defensive skills were widely praised.
These dwarf-pauldrons are light and supple, allowing greater freedom of movement.
This beryl is reputed to have the power to reflect damage back upon the bearer's enemy.
These pauldrons of Edain-make grant the wearer the strength to press forwards during battle.
This handkerchief belonged to Bindo Brockhouse of the Shire. He never believed in Elves or magic… until he met one in the woods above Woodhall.
These pauldrons, crafted under the stars of Elbereth in the cool climes of Lindon, confer upon their wearer greater endurance.
This copper-piece is rumoured to have the ability to give its bearer a silver tongue when bartering.
These pauldrons, crafted in the Grey Mountains, have survived countless years of turmoil.
This bow is rumoured to have once belonged to a great captain of Doriath, before Beleriand fell into the Sea, borne by the long tides to the shores of Middle-earth.
This is one of three bows named after the Winds from which Men oft seek tidings of the world. The West Wind is the wandering Wind.
This bow was once borne by one of the greatest hunters in the Shire. He oft brought down his quarry with a single, well-placed arrow.
This is one of three bows named after the Winds from which Men oft seek tidings of the world. The North Wind blows from the Gate of Kings.
This crossbow was crafted by a great dwarf-smith of the Grey Mountains when the dragons first came out of the North. Unfortunately, a single crossbow could not stop a horde.
This mechanical bow was crafted by the Men of Angmar for use in the wars against the North Kingdom long ago. Perhaps it may be put to the cause of good.
This mechanical bow, crafted in the forges of Carn Dûm, slew many Men of Arnor before it was lost. Now it may be used to avenge the memory of those it slew.
This axe came from the armouries of Khazad-dûm long before it was known as Moria, long before the darkness came.
This axe was used by a brave Bree-man to try and lay to rest the first barrow-wights as they appeared in the old Downs. Unfortunately one brave man was not enough.
This axe was wielded by a guardsman who watched the gates of one of the ancient dwarf-kingdoms which fell to ruin within the Blue Mountains.
It is believed that it was with this axe that Fram slew the mighty dragon Scatha long ago.
This axe, etched with the image of a ship upon the Sea, was forged in memory of Númenor that was.
This axe was borne by a guardsman of Khazad-dûm in the early ages of the world. To what end the guard came is unknown, though some say he awoke Durin's Bane.
This axe was forged by one of the greatest dwarf-smiths of the now-ruined kingdoms which once lay within the heart of the Blue Mountains.
The bit of this dwarf-forged axe has been honed to the finest edge for the greatest effectiveness in battle.
This club was crafted by the Woodmen from wood felled by Orcs. It is believed to grant its bearer the endurance of the forest.
This club was borne across the Misty Mountains by the fathers of the Stoors. It proved that Stone-trolls are not completely impervious to wood.
This club has weathered many battles over the centuries and still has many more to go.
This club was borne by a hobbit-captain in the last battle of Fornost. Legend has it that it was used to slay a great captain of Angmar.
This club was used to protect the leaf-fields of Longbottom against the ruffians stirring trouble in the Southfarthing.
This club is so big that Shire-folk say only a descendant of the Bullroarer Took would be able to wield it.
This club was crafted by a Staddle-hobbit in hopes of becoming a legend in the Midgewater Marshes. He became a legend after he went missing.
This club was crafted by the Woses of the Drúadan Forest in Anórien. It is believed that the cunning of that folk remains in the weapon.
This knife has been carried for generations the dwarf-hunters of the Grey Mountains, but it was lost when the dragons came from the North and drove Durin's Folk away.
This dagger was forged in the kingdom of Arnor to defend against the tyranny of Angmar.
Gilnaith is believed to have been worn at the belt of the last great Elf-king, Gil-galad, as he marched to Mordor with the last great Alliance of Elves and Men.
The blade of this dagger is crafted in such a way as to catch the edge of an opposing weapon, allowing Remmenolf's wielder to more easily parry attacks.
Steadfast was crafted in Dale in the days of Girion. The virtue of this halberd is to renew the bearer's vigour, whilst sapping the strength of the enemy.
This halberd of the Galadhrim was forged to defend the borders of Lothlórien from the Orcs of Moria after the dwarves were driven hence.
This halberd was borne by a door-warden of Meduseld in Edoras long ago. What became of the warden is not written.
This spear was borne by one of the Horse-lords of the Riddermark in elder days for hunting the great boars of Rohan.
This spear was crafted by a hunter from Needlehole for the purpose of ridding Rushock Bog of the monstrous toads which dwell there. You have to be quick to skewer a toad.
This spear was crafted in the North Kingdom of Arnor, before it broke into the three Kingdoms of the North, Arthedain, Cardolan, and Rhudaur. It was lost in the wars with Angmar.
This staff was crafted in Lothlórien to defend against the power of Dol Guldur in the days of the Necromancer.
This staff, brought to Middle-earth from Númenor by a lore-master in service to Elendil, is believed to have the power to renew the strength of its bearer.
This staff was once borne by the Old Took in his 'respectable' days. It was stolen by a nephew who went adventuring.
This staff was borne by the Chief Gate-warden of the White Mountains. It was believed to have the power to drive away the spirits which haunt the White Mountains.
This staff was carried by Blanco Fallohide as he and his brother crossed the Brandywine River into the land now known as the Shire. It was crafted from wood grown east of the Misty Mountains.
This mace was brought with the kindred of Elendil from Númenor of old.
While this mace is heavier than is wont for Elves, it was crafted thus by the smiths of Lindon to cause great hurt.
This Elven mace has been known to cause fatal wounds with but a single blow.
The strength of Hope-bringer renews the spirit of the wielder, despite the shadows which prey upon the heart.
This hammer is one of five sisters forged by the greatest smiths of the dwarf-kingdoms. Forged within the smithies of the Iron Hills, Iron-breaker represents the might of the dwarves.
Though capable of dealing significant damage, Crows-claw was crafted especially as a parrying weapon.

This hammer is one of five sisters forged by the greatest smiths of the dwarf-kingdoms. Forged within the smithies of the Lonely Mountain, Mountain-breaker represents the everlasting endurance of the dwarves.
This hammer is weighted such that it can be brought to bear more quickly.
This hammer was forged by the smiths of the White Mountains to defend their halls from the legendary spirits which haunt the mountain passes.
This hammer was crafted in Tharbad before the town fell into ruin and robbers made their home there.
This sword is light and well-balanced, allowing its wielder to move swiftly and unhindered.
The blows of this sword weaken the wielder's foe, while renewing the strength of the wielder.
Shining boots crafted by Elf-masters of Rivendell.
This sword, forged in the smithies of the Lonely Mountain, is crafted for the strong of arm.
This sword was forged in the smithies of Lindon for use in the war against Sauron in ages past. A virtue has been placed upon it to smite the deadliest of the Dark Lord's minions.
Crafted by Elven-masters for the Battle of the Five Armies.
The weight of this sword allows the wielder to inflict greater damage with stroke.
This sword was crafted in the First Age to fight in the early wars against Morgoth.
This sword was borne by one of the Rohirrim, long before Eorl the Young rode to the aid of Gondor, when his people still dwelt in the north.
This sword of ancient Arnor was borne by the Captain of Amon Sûl until the tower fell to the ravages of Angmar.
This Elven sword has a razor-sharp blade, capable of piercing even the toughest armour.
Hat of Númenórean craftsmanship, light and strong.

An ancient obelisk upon which many names of men have been inscribed. Some are so old as to be faded beyond recognition, others look as if they might have been carved yesterday.

A casting mould used in crafting dwarf-blades of the second age. The craftsmanship is exquisite, but it would probably only survive one more use.
A gold ring embossed with the arms of Arthedain.
A sturdy set of hammer and tongs for use in smithing and smelting metal.
A fine set of woodworking tools.
A set of bowls, spoons, pans and more.
A fine crystal lens, useful in examining various documents.
Finely detailed crafting tools, moulds, clamps and other tools of the jeweler's trade.
Awls, moulds, and tanning supplies for the working of leather.
Hoes, spades, and tools of the farmer's trade.
A heavy hatchet for chopping branches.
This fine armour represents the ancient wisdom of the Elves and pieces of it portray their departure into the West.
These Elven leggings have long protected their wearers through the years from the bite of snakes and other venomous creatures, but they could not save the last from a fiery death.
These leggings, crafted by the Eglain of the Lone-lands, are perfect for slogging through the marshes.
It is believed that this helm of Númenor enables its wearer to see more clearly, allowing him to avoid harm.
These shoes were crafted by the dwarves of the Iron Hills to improve the wearer's agility on the mountain slopes.
This jacket brought to Middle-earth from Númenor has strength enough to protect its wearer from significant injury.
This waistcoat, crafted in Imladris, grants long endurance to its wearer.
This fine armour represents the ancient wisdom of the Elves and pieces of it portray their departure into the West.
These dwarf-leggings have endured quakes and battles through countless years.
This breastplate was worn by a champion of Gondor in the early days of the Stewards.
This helm was worn by a Bree-man who took part in the battle of Fornost. He perished before the end, but his deeds were valorous.
This hat, woven by a tailor from Lake-town, was always a source of courage for its first owner.
These guards are made of mithril, rendering them extremely light. They were forged in Khazad-dûm before the fall of Durin.
These dwarf-leggings were forged in the Iron Hills for the father of Dáin Ironfoot. They were later sent to Thorin's Halls as a gift to Dáin's cousin, but they never arrived.
This helm, forged by the smiths of the Grey Havens, is a strong protection for the wearer.
This suit of Elven armour was forged at the haven of Edhellond for a captain who chose to remain in Middle-earth.
These pauldrons of Dale-make are made to last for many years.
These leggings, crafted by the Elves of Edhellond, are made of a light cloth that allows quick movement.
These shoes, crafted by the Eglain of the Lone-lands, are perfect for slogging through the marshes.
These shoes were crafted by Eglain of the Lone-lands for long, arduous journeys.
This tough shirt, crafted in Thorin's Halls before Thorin Oakenshield departed for the Lonely Mountain, is made such that it may soften blows from falling debris or the attacks of foes.
This robe was woven by the Elves of Mirkwood and allows its wearer to blend more easily into the shadows.
Light cloth gloves of Elven make.
Hooded cloak fashioned from strong, textured fabric.
These pauldrons were once worn by one of Helm the Hammerhand's retainers at the great fortress of Helm's Deep.
This dwarf-helm was made in the halls of the Iron Hills to serve the forebears of Dáin Ironfoot.
These gloves once belonged to a skilled Elven warrior from Edhellond.
These shoes were made in the mountain glades of Lindon and given to a mighty warrior of Gil-galad's host.
This armour was cobbled together by a famous burglar, who sought renown in more than just the burgling arts.
These pauldrons were lost in the Gladden Fields when Isildur and his company were ambushed by Orcs.
These leggings, forged by the men of Tharbad in the days before its ruin, were worn by a warrior who journeyed north to the aid of Fornost long ago.
This helm was worn by one of Glorfindel's Elves as they rode to the aid of Eärnur at Angmar.

This helm was crafted by the men who dwell upon the southern slopes of Ered Nimrais in the shadow of the Paths of the Dead. It was believed to embolden the spirit against the shades which dwelt there.
These shoes, crafted by the Elves of Edhellond, are made of a sturdy cloth to protect the wearer's feet.
This armour was forged for a warrior of the Grey Mountains before the Dragons came. Whoever wore this would be proud to know that a brave heart such as yourself has found it.
Light cloth shoes of Elven make.
This helm was crafted from gold taken from the hoard of Smaug, though it was lost soon after.
These pauldrons were crafted in Lothlórien to combat the shadow which fell upon Dol Guldur.
These uncomfortable gloves from the hills of Rhudaur are stiff enough to provide some protection for the wearer's hands.
This old hat shaded the eyes of many a sluggard throughout the years.
These pauldrons were worn by an Elf of Lindon who voyaged north to seek King Arvedui at the Bay of Forochel.
These leggings were forged by the smiths of Rohan for Helm the Hammerhand in days long past. He wore them to victory at his fortress of Helm's Deep.
This steel helm is rumoured to have been worn by the Father of the Dwarves of the White Mountains, but it has never been proven.
These gauntlets were made by a burglar who desired to keep his fingers.
These leggings from the White Mountains are uncomfortable, but are quite sturdy.
These leggings were crafted by the Dwarves of the Iron Hills to improve the wearer's persistence in battle.
These gloves, crafted by the Snow-men of Forchel, are warm and exquisitely comfortable.
These shoes were crafted by the dwarves of the Blue Mountains for the greatest comfort.
This waistcoat brought from the haven of Edhellond is woven of an extremely tough cloth capable of dulling blades.
Heavy dwarf-scale leggings reinforced against damage.
This armour was forged for a warrior of the Grey Mountains before the Dragons came. Whoever wore this would be proud to know that a brave heart such as yourself has found it.
These leggings, forged in Dale in the days of Girion, are light enough for their wearer to maintain his endurance.
These Elven boots were forged for longevity in the forges of Lindon.
These leggings were crafted by the Dwarves of the Blue Mountains to be light and easy to run in.
The Númenórean captain who wore this helm used it as a symbol of hope for his men.
This dwarf-helm, crafted in the halls of the Grey Mountains, is far more durable than it appears.
These gloves were brought to Middle-earth from Númenor long ere the isle was drowned.
A wandering poet once wore this hat. He found it calming, until a troll convinced him otherwise.
This cloak will not catch on limbs, nor hinder the movement of its wearer.
This armour was forged from the scales of Scatha the Worm, who was slain long ago by the great North-man Fram.
Every captain is known at a glance by his armour, and this set is perhaps one of the most recognizable you have seen. It seems Arnorian in origin.
Cloth shoulder armour of Elven make.
These pauldrons belonged to one of the Riders of Rohan in the early days of the Mark.
These leggings, forged by the Elves of Lindon, are heavier than Elves are wont to wear, but they provide superior protection.

These leggings were forged in the smithies of the White Mountains for one the elder dwarf-kings. This king attempted to seize the eastern Ered Nimrais from the Dead who dwell there, but failed in the end.
This suit of armour is light of weight and forged for freedom of movement, so that the wearer will not tire easily.
These shoes from the White Mountains are not particularly comfortable, but they will wear a very long time.
These dwarf-pauldrons were crafted in the halls of the Grey Mountains with the virtue to grant stamina to their wearer.
This helm came from Imladris in the days following the fall of Eregion. It was worn by an Elven warrior who marched with Gil-galad.
This Bree-hat was reinforced to help protect its wearer, while journeying on the road.
This fine armour was crafted from aurochs hides taken from the great aurochs of the North Downs in tribute to the mighty hunters who acquired the hides.
These pauldrons were forged in the early days of the White Mountain dwarf-hold.
These pauldrons, crafted in Lindon for the wars against Sauron, confer on their wearer the will to continue.
This cloak was made in the land of Lórien and will shield its wearer from the eyes of his enemy.
Leather chest armour of Elven make.
A light Elvish robe that can be used for comfort as well as protection.
These pauldrons were made in the elder days by the Men of Tharbad. The tough material with which they are made provides greater protection than usual.
This cap was once worn by a fool in the court of Gondor, bringing laughter to the hearts of his watchers.
These pauldrons were brought to Middle-earth from Númenor long ere the drowning of that isle.
This shirt was worn by a man of Lake-town who journeyed in peace from Esgaroth through Mirkwood on his way across the Misty Mountains, but was slain by Orcs ere he could cross the High Pass.
The weave of this Bree-waistcoat is extremely sturdy and long-lasting.
This Arnorian robe was worn into battle by a lore-master of Annúminas. Though it did little to protect him, it was light enough to keep him from wearing out.
Cloth chest armour of Elven make.
This suit of armour was worn by Thorin Oakenshield at the Battle of Five Armies and was buried with him beneath the Lonely Mountain. How it came to be abroad is unknown.
These leggings were made in the mountain glades of Lindon and have been worn by many mighty warriors.
A farmer from Bree considered this his lucky hat. His crops were always good, and he always avoided danger. Then he vanished.
This cloak was made by the Elves of Mirkwood and grants its wearer greater Endurance.
This armour, studded with beryls, known also as Elf-stones, is a fine set, crafted by the Elves for a minstrel of great renown.
A light leather and metal helm.
This helm was worn by Anárion, second son of Elendil, as he ruled at Minas Anor at the beginning of the Third Age.
This suit of armour was worn by a warrior from Dale in the days of Girion, before the dragon came.
This armour was cobbled together by a famous burglar, who sought renown in more than just the burgling arts.
Leather shoulder armour of Elven make.
These pauldrons were forged within the smithies of Khazad-dûm for a dwarf who once guarded the Redhorn Gate.
These Elven leggings were forged to afford their wearer greater freedom of movement and were given to an archer from Edhellond as payment for services rendered.
These mighty dwarf-boots were forged in Khazad-dûm When the Orcs first came against the dwarves.
These leggings of Dale-make are perfect for those wishing to be quick.
This light Elven helm is possessed of the virtue to renew and refresh its wearer when at peace.
This hat was brought from Númenor with Elendil and his sons. The wearer was a lore-master of great renown.
This dwarf-robe, woven long ago in the halls of Khazad-dûm for the dwarf-king's chief minstrel, is possessed of great virtues.
This sturdy robe, tailored in Bree, has lasted for many long years and appears to have many good years left in it.
This cloak was made by the Elves of the Grey Havens and will provide its wearer some protection against injury.
Scaled shirt with heavy steel breastplate and long cloth sleeves.
This armour was forged from the scales of Scatha the Worm, who was slain long ago by the great North-man Fram.
A light Westernesse robe that can be used for comfort as well as protection.
Helm of the Horse-lords of the Riddermark.
This helm was once worn by an archer of Mirkwood who ventured into the realm of the Necromancer.
These gauntlets were forged by the smiths of the Grey Mountains for use against the dragons of the North.
These dwarf-pauldrons were crafted not only for protection, but longevity as well.
This hat was woven in the land of Dorwinion, renowned for its extraordinary wine.
Ancient armour of the ancestors of the Rohirrim.
These gauntlets were forged by the Elves of Imladris for use in the wars against Sauron.
These gauntlets were forged in the smithies of Lothlórien for the defence of the Wood against the shadow of Dol Guldur.
These dwarf-boots were forged in the Grey Mountains as part of an armour suit used against the dragons.
This jacket, made in the glades of Lothlórien, has a superior weave to most others for longer wear.
This hat, oft worn by lore-masters through the years, seems to give the scholarly an unhealthy touch of courage.
Through lost arts, thin iron strands were woven into this hat, making it stronger than most.
This cloak was made by the Elves of Imladris and will afford its wearer greater courage.
This fine armour was crafted from aurochs hides taken from the great aurochs of the North Downs in tribute to the mighty hunters who acquired the hides.
This helm was worn by Eorl the Young while he dwelt still in the North.
This dwarf-armour was worn by a captain of the White Mountains, who perished at last when he sought treasure on the Paths of the Dead.
Dwarves are most at peace when working the stone of the earth, and this shirt, crafted in the halls of Grey Mountains reflects that attitude.
Armour of Elven-make, finely tooled in the Dark Forest.
The original owner of these pauldrons attached many tiny bells to them, and his foes learned to fear the sound.
These gauntlets were brought from Númenor in the days of Elendil, and they are still strong, despite the years upon them.
These boots were forged in the smithies of Imladris for a fleet-footed archer who marched with Gil-galad and Elendil against Sauron.
This dwarf-armour was forged of mithril in the days prior to the fall of Khazad-dûm.
This mithril coat was forged by the Elves of Lothlórien in the days of peace between Moria and the Wood.
These gloves, crafted by the Elves of Lindon, were worn by a great warrior, who marched in the host of Gil-galad against Barad-dûr.
This hat, strung with many jewels, offers its wearer protection from ill-aimed blows.
This robe was fashioned for a dwarf-smith of the Blue Mountains, tailored to survive the smith's arduous labours.
This helm was worn by one of the ancient kings of the Grey Mountains, though the dragons eventually overcame him.
These dwarf-gauntlets were forged in the smithies of the Blue Mountains ere the fall of Beleriand long ago.
These pauldrons of Númenor are strong enough to dull any blade which strikes them.
These Elven gloves, crafted in Mirkwood, are reinforced for extra durability.
This cloak is exceptionally sturdy and durable and will wear long.
Every captain is known at a glance by his armour, and this set is perhaps one of the most recognizable you have seen. It seems Arnorian in origin.
This armour, studded with beryls, known also as Elf-stones, is a fine set, crafted by the Elves for a minstrel of great renown.
This helm of the Rohirrim was worn by one of Eorl's lancers at the Battle of the Field of Celebrant.
These boots were made by the Eglain of the Lone-lands for one of their Elders so that his feet would be protected from all harm as they scavenged the swamp-ruins.
This armour of Westernesse saw its glory-days on the plains of Gorgoroth as Elendil and Gil-galad marched upon Barad-dûr.
This hat was all that remains of Livina Broadleaf's dowery. It is also all that remains of Livina.
The wearer of this hat always felt light on his feet.
This robe was brought across the Sea by a lore-master of Númenor in elder days. It is said to have a virtue to protect its wearer from harm.
This robe, tailored in Dorwinion, is very light and supple, allowing its wearer great freedom of movement.
This robe, woven by the Elves of Edhellond, is said to confer upon its wearer a great strength of spirit.
These leggings were forged by a warrior of the Blue Mountains who was terrified of spiders.
These gloves from the Lonely Mountain are extremely light and supple.
These shoes of Dale-make are perfect for the light of foot.
This robe, worn by a lore-master of the Lonely Mountain in elder days, grants its wearer extraordinary stamina and endurance.

When Ión was young, his first helm was this one which brought him many victories. While you wear it, Ión says you even look a little like him.
Gloves of this nature are used when polishing precious gems and metals.
How these gloves found their way here and to such an appropriate task you have no idea.
Darri wouldn't hear any arguments about temperature or decency concerns when he provided these as a reward.
Tirelessly defending the miners, Thalfar's shoulders never slump.
Gansi would be honoured if you wore his cloak during your exploits throughout Moria.
You were told that this footwear is guaranteed to make you run faster and jump higher.
Túbi claims to have knocked out five Orcs with these gloves.
Used by the dwarves of old when doing manual labour within the Cooling Chamber.
Arnod encouraged you to live your life mindful of the past and to tell your story to your children.
Used to protect workers from falling debris.
Gamli was happy to give you these leggings as a reward after finding bugs crawling around in the pockets.
Having defeated Tudur in personal combat, the remaining Dunlendings may get the message to return to their lands.
Not named because they are made from gredbyg, but because they provide as much protection as a grodbog hide does.
These shoulders will support you as walls support the ceiling.
Given time your efforts should restore Glâd Ereg to what it once was.
You have helped shield the Company from unwanted attention. All that remains is to hope they make it through Moria.
While it has seen better days, this shield's craftmanship is nonetheless exquisite.
A magnificent shield awarded to you for helping reassemble the statue.
Perhaps it is just your imagination, but this shield smells of the scent-glands you collected for Thórhall.
Crafted long ago from the wood of a fallen holly-tree.
The surface of this shield slightly reflects light making the darkness a bit easier to bear.
Inufileg brought this with her all the way from Rivendell, but has gifted it to you.
The favoured axe of Túbi Thickfist.
The angle of this blade is perfect for carving through tough shells.
In the right hands, Javelins can bring down mighty foes.
This may be the first of these Uruk-hai you have defeated, but you suspect it will not be the last.
Able to fly faster than one can run, many Wardens often find it easier to let their weapon chase their quarry.
This rune-stone is warm to the touch.
This rune-stone is cold to the touch.
This rune-stone sends tingles through your fingers as you touch it.
Whether chieftain or minion, a dead goblin still looks like a dead goblin.
You have accomplished great deeds here, though you wonder what awaits you in the future?
A quick thrust through the heart ends the reign of the worm.
Pierce the black heart of foul creatures and light will return.
Has hewn many goblins as evidenced by its many notches.
Siggir claimed that this sword was best when used against goblins, though you suspect he was just trying to get you to do more work.
Hamall entrusted you with his walking stick.
While there is more work yet to be done, you have performed a honourable service for the Elves.
When the crazed goblin Gîmog met his end you were the one introducing him to it.
This blade has carved a story or two into history.
Cleaving the wings from the vile mervyl seems to be what this weapon was made for.
Let this weapon serve as a none-too-gentle reminder to all goblins that dwarven treasure is not for the taking.
While it pained you to kill a living tree, it was necessary to stop the spies of the Enemy.
Given to you as a reward on the express condition that you use it to smash any goblins you see.
Crafted by himself, Lithuilas says he has never missed a shot with this bow.
Siggir encouraged you to use this bow to slay many more goblins in your travels.
This crossbow has been used to effectively count Warg-riders throughout Moria.
Deception is a powerful weapon, though an axe is quite powerful too.
A fungal spore gathered from a fallen Globsnaga Orc.

An extremely durable necklace fashioned from silver and covered in thick, polished turquoise stones.
The brooch is solid gold and in the shape of a snail. The surface is decorated with diamonds.

The branch appears burnt at one end but otherwise untouched by the fire.

Used by members of the Eglain who tend to the wounds of the hidden people of the Lone-lands, this sword is crafted by weaponsmiths amongst the Eglain. Its blade is sharp and honed to assist the Eglan-mender who wields the sword in battle.

Used by members of the Eglain who stand and battle the evils that threaten the Lone-lands, this axe is crafted by weaponsmiths amongst the Eglain. Its blade is weighted well to assist the Eglan-vanguard who wield the axe in battle.
These halberds are wielded in battle by those who watch over the battlefront. The Eglan-guards are a steadfast group who use these weapons with great skill.
When faced with a threat the Eglan-defenders wield these swords as they stand strong in the face of their enemy.
Eglain who fight are all given the dagger of the soldier. This is a blade meant for the close combat work needed when fighting in hard battles.
When range is necessary for battling foes, the Eglan-warden uses his javelin to great effect.
These stones are crafted by the eldest and most knowledgable of the Eglain. They are used to scribe their language for future generations.
Those scholars amongst the Eglain often carry such staves taken from nature and adorned with beautiful beryls.
Survival is the mainstay of the hidden folk in the Lone-lands and providers often use bows to strike down their meals from a distance.
These shields are used by the Eglan-wardens while they fight battles.
Eglan defenders use these shields as they fight to protect what is theirs.
These shields are used by the Eglain along with the swords of their menders while they fight battles.

Overcoming setbacks is as simple as remembering a bright and sunny day. Using this item will remove dread caused by defeat in areas untouched by the brewing war.

Recalling those moments where you were most at peace can help you overcome the most difficult moments. Using this will remove dread caused by defeat in areas where there are only hints of the brewing war.
There are no visions so dark that they cannot be overcome. Using this item will remove dread caused by defeat in areas directly affected by the war.

There is always hope, even in the darkest hour. Find your strength in the freedom shared by all people. Using this item will remove dread caused by defeat in areas where the Enemy servants are strongest.

Oh boy, oh boy! A gift box! You sure hope it is full of First Age Legendary Items and armour from Dâr Narbugud!
Fishing poles will help the Eglain to survive as they can use them to fish among the few ponds found throughout the Lone-lands.
Recent events in the Lone-lands have robbed the Eglain of the materials necessary for their livelihood.
The threat of disease is ever present in the Lone-lands and the Eglain wish to prepare themselves for the dangers ahead.
If the spiders in the Lone-lands do poison members of the Eglain, then they need some way to remove the poison.
Poison from the spiders is a very real threat to the Eglain and they would appreciate ruby rings of willpower to assist them in defending themselves from the spiders' poison.
These cloaks will be used to restock the cloth and leather goods that the Eglain have lost in recent weeks.
Throwing hatchets are used by the Eglain to hunt food throughout the Lone-lands and they have put out a general call for them.

Bingo's manuscript so far covers his call to adventure and contains a record of his journey through the Shire, Bree-land, the Lone-lands, and the Trollshaws.
Meat from the glen-hinds and glen-bucks in the Trollshaws would make a good meal for a lynx, and doesn't even need to be cooked.
Several pages of Bingo's manuscript describe his initial experiences across the Brandywine Bridge and tracking down the sons and daughters of his cousin Prisca in Buckland.

This hand-drawn map contains many small pictures of interesting locations throughout Eriador, and seems to have been painstakingly crafted.
It is a wonder that Bingo was able to condense his belongings into just a few satchels, but if he forgets to bring the satchels it does not matter!
Several pages of Bingo's journal describe his plan to host a dinner party for his neighbours, and the discovery of the map that set him out on his journey.

Bingo's manuscript is written in the messy hand of someone not yet accustomed to writing so many pages. It covers his departure from the Shire, the search for Prisca Boffin's children, and leaves off just before arriving at the house of Tom Bombadil.

This sculpture was carved by Bhai-buri-Ghân before he was slain by Orcs, and it was gifted to you by his brother Khôr-buri-Ghân, who was grateful for your help in discovering this unseen side of his brother. It was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it.

This stone key is very angular and covered in runes that mark it as unlocking a door somewhere in Khazad-dûm. The time it spent in Mordor has added to its corruption, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.
This small shard has splintered off the tusk of a porcine animal. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

This small sculpture is carved in the shape of a squat, humanoid figure, reminiscent of the Púkel-men that guard the road to Dunharrow. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

This key was used to seal away an archive in Khazad-dûm, but the holder of the key was slain and the key he bore was taken into Mordor. Forgotten, the dwarves that were sealed away survived as long as they could, but came in time to a sad end. You unlocked the door, and in so doing cleansed the key's corruption.
This brooch of bone belonged to a Lossoth man named Oiva, and it was gifted to you by his widow Pinja when you cleansed it of the corruption that had fastened to it in Mordor.

This cup is fashioned of clay used by the hill-men of Rhudaur during the days of their ascendancy, and it has a single blood-red ruby mounted on one side. The time it spent in Mordor has added to its corruption, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

These seeds were entrusted to Trotsiv of the Earth-kin, and he protected them from those who would do them harm. Though the pouch was brought into Mordor, and corruption ensnared it, the seeds within could not be ruined or destroyed, and now you have cleansed it of that evil.

This shard of tusk splintered from the tusk of the Great Boar of Everholt, which slew and was slain by King Folca of Rohan. The Boar-tribe of the Eastfold worshipped the tusk-shard, but it was taken into Mordor against their wishes. It has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it.

This needle of the Uch-lûth travelled many leagues within the body of the Orc that slew Deilur more than fifty years ago, before it finally meted her justice upon him. The corruption that affixed to the needle in Mordor has been cleansed by returning it to the land that Deilur called home.

This small badge or medal is reminiscent of the type that is sometimes worn by guards at their posts, and Gandalf believes that this one was worn by a guard of High King Elendil at Annúminas. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.
This badge was worn by a guard of High King Elendil at the Bridge of Ariant, in Annúminas. The badge was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it.

This bone fragment may have splintered from a spear-point such as those used by the tribes of Enedwaith and Dunland. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

This sculpture was carved by Bemwin, a skilled artist who loved the champion Darothild and made this representation of her shortly before she faced the Red-maid, and perished. It was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it.
This brooch is made of bone and encircled by a curved piece of what appears to be antler. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

This sceptre Is about two feet long and holds an orb at one clawed end, near which faint markings can be seen. Gandalf believes this sceptre is an heirloom of the Kingdom of Cardolan. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

This small sculpture of a woman is carved from bone or tusk. One hand is raised as if in warning, and in the other she holds a spear ready to throw at an unseen foe. The time it spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.

This leather bag is sealed with a strap of cord tied in a simple-looking knot, but the knot resists any attempt to untie it. The time the pouch spent in Mordor has corrupted it, and now it radiates a feeling of great evil.
This cup was used by Rhudauran priests in their vile ceremonies, but it has been cleansed of its evil.

This sceptre belonged to a forgotten prince of Cardolan, who stood against the men of Carn Dûm but was slain. The sceptre was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it.
Many are the mysteries that remain locked away behind doors in Khazad-dûm, and even dwarves cannot say what might lie behind them.

This needle of the Uch-lûth travelled many leagues within the body of the Orc that slew Deilur more than fifty years ago, before it finally meted her justice upon him. The corruption that affixed to the needle in Mordor has been cleansed by returning it to the land that Deilur called home. Elrond has imbued it with the Light of Eärendil, and believes it will help you banish the shadows of Mordor.

This sceptre belonged to a forgotten prince of Cardolan, who stood against the men of Carn Dûm but was slain. The sceptre was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it. Elrond has imbued it with the Light of Eärendil, and believes it will help you banish the shadows of Mordor.

This sculpture was carved by Bemwin, a skilled artist who loved the champion Darothild and made this representation of her shortly before she faced the Red-maid, and perished. It was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it. Elrond has imbued it with the Light of Eärendil, and believes it will help you banish the shadows of Mordor.

This shard of tusk splintered from the tusk of the Great Boar of Everholt, which slew and was slain by King Folca of Rohan. The Boar-tribe of the Eastfold worshipped the tusk-shard, but it was taken into Mordor against their wishes. It has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it. Elrond has imbued it with the Light of Eärendil, and believes it will help you banish the shadows of Mordor.

This cup was used by Rhudauran priests in their vile ceremonies, but it has been cleansed of its evil. Elrond has imbued it with the Light of Eärendil, and believes it will help you banish the shadows of Mordor.

This sculpture was carved by Bhai-buri-Ghân before he was slain by Orcs, and it was gifted to you by his brother Khôr-buri-Ghân, who was grateful for your help in discovering this unseen side of his brother. It was taken into Mordor, but has returned and been cleansed of the evil that corrupted it. Elrond has imbued it with the Light of Eärendil, and believes it will help you banish the shadows of Mordor.

But war, plague, and other attritions weakened the Kingdom of Men, and in time, the Watch on Mordor faltered.
By cunning, force, and treachery did Ugrukhôr, the Captain of the Pit seize Durthand and Udûn. The tower he made his own and renamed to Durthang, the Dark Oppression.
Deep in Anglach, with great works and dark sorceries, Grond, the fearsome battering ram which broke the gates of Minas Tirith, was forged.
New Morgul blades and other evil implements were hewn from the cursed iron mined from the Pit and hidden away in dark places. Who knows what evil is still locked away in these mountains.
The Captain strengthened the fortifications of Udûn, restored the old, and built anew. Anglach arose and Mornaur towered under his command.
Sauron returned, and once again the forges blazed. Great stockpiles of Orc-arms were smithied, but the old alloys and dark enchantments were remembered, too.
Timeless and changed were the nine Nazgûl; their old names forgotten, their old titles and reigns turned to dust. New names they would earn, for their deeds in Sauron's service.
Then upon the pinnacle of Barad-dûr did Sauron stand, rightful lord of all. He raised the One Ring high, spoke dark words, and a wreath of shadow and storm were all about the Tower's top.
Long in sight, deep in cunning, did he don the One Ring and with his newfound power made war against the Elves and therein seized the Nine rings, and the Seven.
The Bane of Rhûn, The Woe of Khand, and The Cursed Rider did the Easterling Chieftains become. Their rings are Sâkhla, The Cruel One, Adâsh, the Foe-maker, and Orôm, the Warmonger.
One by one the Nine Kings abased themselves before their Lord and Master, for they were Nazgûl, Ringwraiths, now, and all marvelled at the One Ring's might.
Three rings of the Nine yet remained, and these he bestowed upon Númenórean Men, proud and tall, who had bowed before him well and faithfully since times of old.
The Lord of the Nazgûl, who wields the sorcerous power of the ring Ûri, the Heart-stopper, was titled Witch-king of Angmar, and justly so, for Angmar quivered under his wrathful gaze.
Deep in Sammath Naur, amongst the fire and the dark, in the forge of his own devising, the Dark Lord wrought the One Ring. The One to rule all others.
Thus were the Nazgûl, the Great Lord Sauron's most powerful servants, made. Each in his own keep in Mordor they dwelled, and in Minas Morgul they gathered, a fell and terrible host!
With the raising of the Ring, the Nine Kings, all upon their thrones, were called henceforth to the Dark Tower and lo! they were become wraiths and servants of my Lord.
Then to Rhûn and Harad Sauron roamed, gifting six of the Nine Rings to kings and chieftains, yoking peoples and armies under his command. Seven to Dwarf-lords, in their hidden halls.
The Grim Southron, The High Sorcerer of Harad, and The Forsaken Reaver were the Southrons named. Their rings are Jûru, the Herald of Mourning, Mêbat, the Mirth-eater, and Khânto, the Pain-giver.
And the Númenórean kings became The Black Blade of Lebennin and The Gloom of Nurn, wielding Sapthân, the Foolstone, and Nitîr, Terror's Sting.

Thus, as Lord Sauron tells it, Shelob became his ‘cat.’ And so, she kept Mordor free of its foes for many years, all for the price of few Orkish sacrifices and a supply of curious or unwary travellers.
Centuries later, when at last Lord Sauron came to Mordor, he knew at once that something terrible and powerful lurked in the Mountains of Shadow.
In time, she became as Ungoliant, and her hunger grew insatiable. She spawned numberless spiders and crawling terrors both to serve her... and to feed her.

As Lord Sauron reminds me, Shelob serves no whims but her own. At times, a single Orc can sate her hunger, but when she desires it, she will devour a company of Orcs and betray their foolish trust in that imagined bargain.
Ungwetári, the last child of Ungoliant - this is the name he has chosen for her, but her Ladyship has been known by many names, and even he has not learned her true name.

In Shelob's wrath, her children flooded the passages beneath the tower, killing all they encountered. However, she relented before her children reached the cellars of Cirith Ungol - a mercy later repaid in sacrifices by Orcs seeking safe passage.
Driven only by her hunger, Shelob desired neither an alliance nor conquest, and to Lord Sauron's amusement, she chased him from her lair in the mountains.
Lord Sauron soon learned that Shelob dwelt within them, and in his wisdom, he sought her aid in conquering the Elves and Men of the West.
Long before Lord Sauron came to Mordor, and long before the first stone of Barad-dûr was cast, she lived - a creature of evil in the form of spider.
When first she fled from Beleriand, Shelob came to the Greenwood. It was there she spawned the first of her vile children, and together they devoured it from within.
Indeed, woe be the day when Shelob's hunger grows too great, for when at last she comes before Lord Sauron, he shall destroy her utterly.
At my begging, he has shared with me his knowledge of Lhingris, for beneath the towers and Orc-paths is the shadowed spider-haunt, the web-rift, and Ungwetári's kingdom of filth.
Indeed, through his wisdom, she became the guardian of the western pass into Mordor. In return, he sent her his prisoners and lesser Orcs to feast on.
After returning to Barad-dûr, Lord Sauron considered destroying her, but he soon realized Shelob and her viciousness might still serve him, wittingly or not...
It was then she came to the Mountains of Shadow, and upon its dark peaks and within its cavernous depths, she felt a grim familiarity. Thus, it is there she has made her home ever since...
To the Alashi of Mordor, she was Tor-Kralicha. To the Orcs, she was once Takhborkhlob, but now she is known to most by another name: Shelob.
Once she dwelt in the Mountains of Terror with the nameless horrors of that lost Age, but when its peaks were drowned, Shelob alone escaped the ruin that consumed the rest of Ungoliant's children.
In the year that Lhaereth unleashed the Great Plague, the Orcs of Cirith Ungol sought to expand the great tower's tunnels, and they foolishly delved into her lair.
Ghâsh-hai, that's what we've become - me and the boys left living after all the fire and falling stone. We are strong - stronger than we've ever been, with arms and bones of flame.
Here's what you get for poking your nose where it shouldn't go. That Urudanî woman had some slaves digging into the floor of the runed chamber, and next thing you know, it was flames everywhere!
So imagine my surprise when at last I thought I'd found my way out of all the flames and debris, and there Urudanî was!
Ah, but the heat down below. You'd think we were digging into Mount Doom itself! The slaves keep collapsing and asking for water. We have a good laugh at them then whip them back to work.
And strangest of all, we still serve the Eye. Or at least, that's what our new master says. All commands come down from him to Urudanî. Nar! Orders are orders, that's what I've always said.
Well to this day I'll never quite know what happened next. There was a roaring voice, and Urudanî's, all defiant as ever. Whatever it was, she fought it and I don't think she won.
There's runes carved all around, on the walls, the floor, the ceiling. Mistress Urudanî finds them interesting enough. If it were up to me, we'd leave them well enough alone.
We serve a new lord now, that's what she told me. And we must be suited to the task. That's when I felt the searing heat rip through me like so many jagged, burning blades.

Me and my boys are taking orders from that Urudanî Stonemaiden. You can smell the stink of arrogance on all these Black Númenórean types. She's got us off in Talath Úrui, digging an underground fortress out of the Mithram.
Strength and fire aside, we Ghâsh-hai and Lady Urudanî are still at it, if you can believe it: building the citadel of Nargroth. The work's nearly done.
Well those slaves were ash faster than you could cut a throat, and not a few Orcs and Uruks, too.
She was Urudanî - and not Urudanî. I can't find a plainer way to say it! She was wreathed in flame. No, she was made of flame. And when she bade me halt, I sure as well did it!
The construction on the upper floors has started, but something happened today. We seem to have dug into a large chamber, separate from the main cavern.
There was still fire and heat everywhere in that wreckage, mind you, and most of the Orcs and slaves were dead as roast pigs. I reckoned our fool of a headmistress was too.
Their towers taken, their watch weakened, Gondor lowered its blade from Mordor's neck and crouched cravenly behind its shield. All this from Lhaereth's Great Plague.
And then, at long last, sisters, our lady found it: the affliction the Dark Lord had asked of her, waster of kingdoms, bane of armies, the Great Plague.
Our Lady Lhaereth toiled in Seregost and wandered the woods of the Broken Vale, sowing plagues and reaping miasmas, pestilences, and deadly venoms.
To the vast vat Lhaereth called her bats, sleek of pelt and dark as night. Upon their wings she cast the disease, and sent them forth beyond the mountains to the world.
In the south, the Great Plague raged across Ithilien and Anórien both, and by the time all was done, had claimed the lives of paupers, knights, bread-bakers, and kings.
Over centuries and ages Lhaereth served and stayed true, and in reward for this Sauron built among the trees of the Broken Vale: Seregost, the Blood-fort.
Sing with me sisters, of our Lady of Blight. Sing of her works, her loyalty, her hunger, and her strength.
Slowly, wonderously, the land changed. Trees blistered and wept, streams ran dark and then red, new things limped and anguished there. Broken Vale no more, it was Agarnaith, the Bloody Gore.
Sing praise to the Lady of Blight, oh my sisters, and tell when the Dark Lord bade her brew up dread diseases to lay low whole kingdoms and arméd hosts.
The hateful Men of Gondor were thinned and driven from their walls and towers. All that they left - Moon Fort and River Palace - the Dark Lord took.
In the distant detphs of time, before us, before Modor, memory whispers of her first poisons, concocted in service to Sauron, laying low rivals and foes.
Sing of the Great Plague that went before any other and made all Sauron's conquests possible.
These are names, O Sisters, of lands where Lhaereth's great plague laid waste: Rhovanion and Gondor, the remnants of Arnor, the northern kingdoms of Cardolan and Arthedain.
In the northern lands, between the Plague and the Witch-king, toppled were kingdoms of Men, their vestiges scattered and fled.
Sing of our beloved mother, Lhaereth the Stained, truest and deadliest and first of them all.

By His command, I devised pains and torments unequalled in any of the Ages of the world.
But on the day the Mountain was rent asunder and its fires cascaded, when the iron walls of Naerband became not just a prison, but an oven.
Before the Mountain raged, I was called Thraknûl. I was the warden of Naerband, the greatest of Lord Sauron's prisons.
I have much to learn if I am to become Shakh Thraknûl, and surpass the Dark Lord in the arts of pain. I need some new captives.
Before the Mountain raged, I was the master of all that transpired within the iron walls of the Direhold. I was the greatest of the Dark Lord's torturers.
A record of the lost lore of Naerband.
When the screams of the roasting doomed filled the air, I beheld that savage masterwork and knew that Sauron, even in death and ruin, was truly the master.

To the East, the Nazgûl had spied the Dwarf-kingdoms in possession of the Rings Tínya and Tulcya left in ruin, but they ventured no nearer for they sensed an ancient, terrible power lurking within each of the dwarves' broken halls.

With the Ring-drakes imprisoned, only Úrya and Vanya remained lost. The Lord of the Nazgûl soon revealed that a great Worm had survived the breaking of Thangorodrim. Desperate to escape the wrath of the Elves in the Elder Days, the Worm had sought shelter in the depths of the Ered Luin.

Thus, the great Worm was cast into Glurnákh, the Pit of Greed. For countless years, the Weeping Warrior brought his greatest tortures upon each of the Ring-drakes, but none yielded the Rings. Neither death nor mercy shall be granted to them, not before they surrender the Rings of Power.

Seven years...a mere seven years, and I heard the truth in Sauron's words. Gil-galad had left me to die, and Sauron in His kindness wrought for me a new form and granted me a place among His greatest servants. Seven years, and He was defeated...but He will return.

And so, the Lord of the Nazgûl granted the Weeping Warrior the Dwarf-ring, Sindya, to draw the Worm from the Ered Luin. Powerless to resist his greed, the great Worm followed the Weeping Warrior into the East. When at last the Worm tired in his pursuit, he fell broken before the Ephel Dúath.
Four of the Seven remained lost and hidden in the Dwarf-kingdoms of Middle-earth, and so it was that the Lord of the Nazgûl ordered one of the Gúrzyul, the Weeping Warrior, to find them.

As Sauron had willed it, the Rings could not be unmade by dragon-fire. Thostír and Hrímil were soon subdued, and the Weeping Warrior dragged them beyond the Lithannon into the deepest dungeons of the Mordath. Thus, Tínya and Tulcya were returned to Mordor.

Indeed, it was Dragons that had laid claim to Tínya and Tulcya. A fire-drake, Thostír the Rank, and a cold-drake, Hrímil Frost-heart, had destroyed the Dwarf-kingdoms of the eastern mountains, and knowingly or not, they swallowed the Rings of Power as well as the Dwarf-kings who wielded them.

Long had the great Worm remained hidden in the Ered Luin, indeed long enough to be forgotten, but as the hoards of those wielding Úrya and Vanya grew, so too did his greed. Heedless of all peril, the Worm sacked the Dwarf-kingdoms and devoured the last of the Seven.

Long after Sauron's fall, the Lord of the Nazgûl decreed that it was His will to gather the Seven Rings to Mordor. Sindya and Taurya had been wrested from the unworthy fingers of Dwarf-kings in the East, but none in Mordor -- not even the Nazgûl -- dared to seek the Ring of Durin, Angya.

You who failed in battle, who failed in strategy, in diplomacy, in foresight - in all but vainglorious strutting - I have you now, Dulgabêth, right where you belong.
You, husband me and rule Mordor together in Sauron's place? Ah ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha.
You have your wish, Dulgabêth, my dear. You will rule Mordor with me. Not by my side, it is true, but at my heel.
Know that I am of the first days and last of my kind. It is I who was worthy to be his bride, stand next to him, give him an heir. And remind me: why were you worthy?
Banners of the white tree crawl all over Gorgoroth. If you are so worthy of the throne, do something about it while I arrange the meeting of our peers.
Forgive me, Dulgabêth. I was over-hasty and in my grief and loss, cruel. Be my consort and king. Together, we shall conquer and rule.
Welcome to Seregost, O Black Word, Mouth of Sauron, Red and Scarred of Face, simpering wretched fool. Did you really think I would wed the likes of you?
Yes, once again I insist we stand before what remains of the Dark Lord's lieutenants and sanctify our troth. Or would you have them band together and war against us?
You are the Mouth of Sauron and will talk. Very well. You wish to talk of heirs? One was promised me by the Dark Lord himself after the war was won.
Dulgabêth, Dulgabêth. I am far too shaken by the loss of our dear lord Sauron and our utter defeat for all this talk of rightful 'heirs'. Save it.

A missive for King Thorin III written by Erna of Dale.
Long ago, there lived a simple archer named Bródda. One day, he came across the Dwarf-king Thrór beset by Orcs, and with his arrows saved the Dwarf-king's life.
Where dwarves toil tirelessly, dragons sleep. What dwarves have mined and wrought, dragons steal. What dwarves barter and bestow, dragons hoard. Truly, they are our natural foes.
Roused from slumber, Smaug took to the sky, and all the Lake-folk would have died but for your great grandsire, named as you are: Bard.
What memories remain of those first years are but fragments. The emerald necklace was lost in war, given in marriage, tainted by treachery, and cast aside in sorrow.
Thus an ancient bond was reforged. The eternal story of Elves and dwarves took its familiar path: friendship, distrust, strife, and then, betimes, friendship again.
It was then that Bard, the leader of Men, did the wise and unthinkable: he broke apart the necklace, handing its gold to the dwarves and to the Elves its gems.
To Khazad-dûm we retreated then, but at last the wakened dragons came and found us there. With the aid of Elves and Men, we bested them, though the cost was great, and for a time knew peace.
Great were the gifts of the new Dwarf-king, Dáin Ironfoot, not least among them new Black Arrows, thrice forged, one for each new Lord of Dale.
Now Thrór II built anew in Erebor, and Grór his brother in the Iron Hills. Our dreams were dead or abandoned, but in time Smaug the Golden awoke and to the Lonely Mountain came.
To Erebor from Mirkwood we came, armed, righteous, bent on reclaiming what was ours. I do not like to think what might have happened, if true enemies had not appeared.
Many years went by, and Bain, Brand's grandson, came out of the woods to be an archer of the Lake-town guard, like his distant ancestor before him.
After the slaying of Smaug, Bard's true lineage was revealed, and so he was named Bard the Bowman, new king of new-built Dale.
Smaug's Desolation fell over the vale. Men fled to Lake-town and the dwarves fled farther. Geirjarn became known as Girion, his sad and shameful tale spread far and wide.
Listen, and you shall hear the tale of strife and friendship between Elves and dwarves, circling back over the long years, in the shape of a single emerald necklace.
Years flowed by once more, and we tended to our woodland realm, forgetting friendship, emeralds, and grievances for the time. Yes, years ran together until one day, everything changed.

The tale of Smaug in Erebor, and how upon Thorin Oakenshield's return, Smaug woke and was slain, is well enough known in these times. I will say only: let this be the last Dragon and last of our sorrows.
King Thrór promised such a gift to each Lord of Dale. Trade grew and thrived between Men and dwarves, and for seven more lords, seven more Black Arrows were forged.
It was a man, Fram, son of Frumgar, Chief of the Éothéod, who ended the Dragon Scatha. A great deed to echo through the ages, and a dragon's hoard as prize.
It was given to him by Men, Thrór said. Men chanced upon it in some troll-hoard, he claimed. I was wroth and had no ears for such tales.
And, like all of Dwarf-kind's greatest sorrows, the curse of Dragons was brought on by ourselves, and cost us all we dreamed and held most dear.
In a time of quiet, when the new king, Dáin I thought all safe, when the Men of the Éothéod were off at war, then the dragons struck, and much was lost.
A gift the emerald necklace was, given freely in times of good will. But friendship, far more fragile than any metal or gem, did not endure.
Time went on. To the Great Greenwood we came, and, sorrow and misfortune ever at our heels, finally to caverned Felegoth, near Erebor, and so, near to dwarves.
Perhaps the age of Men is truly come. Or so it seems to me when the greatest wisdom is to break what you hold dear and to loose your shackles with forgetfulness.
And so this arrow was forged for you, my son. May you never need it, yet keep it well, for some distant day, it may save us all.
The Cold-drake Vethúg Wintermind slayed both King Dáin I and his son, Frór. Their Grey Kingdom was lost, and we fled again, tears in our eyes, to return north no more.
The Battle of Five Armies it is called, but there were only two sides in that hour: Elves, Men, and dwarves against the throngs of evil, until the Eagles came.
Brandjarn took the name Brand, hiding all his lineage for shame of his father's failing. And so the Black Arrow passed secretly from father to son, father to son.
Many are the enemies of dwarves: goblins, Wargs, spiders, Orcs. But oldest and greatest of our foes, yes, maybe greater even than Durin's Bane, are dragons.
Time went and our dreams of the North would not die. So yet again, in the days of Thorin I, to the Grey Mountains we ventured again.
Centuries of peace passed, and the memory of dragons faded. So it was that to the Grey Mountains we sojourned a second time, unknowing that the dragons who had lived and fled lay slumbering there.

Now the Lord of Dale when Smaug attacked was Geirjarn, third of his name. Seven Black Arrows he loosed upon that worm, and each fell short of its mark, the last leaving only a scratch, before he perished in the flames.
Now much of Scatha's hoard was taken from Durin's Folk, and so a messenger was sent to the Men of the Éothéod, begging our share.
Father to son and father to son again the Black Arrow was secretly passed, until the day the dragon sleeping within the mountain awaked.
Thus was Bródda made Lord of Dale, and by the Dwarf-King Thrór gifted the name Geirjarn Ironbolt and a Black Arrow, thrice forged, hard enough to pierce through stone.
Gweriamir we named that necklace then, the Jewel of Betrayal, and no sign of it was seen or heard for years beyond counting.

On just such a peace-weaving visit did I come to Thrór's mountain halls. The feast was set, words of courtesy prepared - and then he stood, where upon his breast I saw the Gweriamir, gleaming green and gold!
This time, the dragons, whose lives and memories are longer than ours, bided their time and waited.
For it was we, of Durin's Folk, who woke the great dragons in times of old, and in so doing lost the Grey Mountains that we called home.
It was a necklace of ancient make, wrought by the dwarves of old. Fine and gleaming was the gold, encrusted with five hundred perfect glittering emeralds, maybe more. Perfect, wondrous, radiant.
The news came: the dragon was slain, there was a king under the mountain. And that day we remembered - remembered friendship, grievances, and debt.
Fire around him and dragon above, Bard stood just as Girion had done long before. Yet Bard's aim was true, and his one Black Arrow struck Smaug down.
After the battle, the dragon's hoard was divied up, and though I would have forfeited all our share for it, the Gweriamir went not to Elves but to Men.
What few knew was that one Black Arrow survived. Eight Lords, eight arrows. Did you count? It fled the fires with Brandjarn, Girion's son, who survived.
What was their reply? A necklace made of Scatha's teeth and nothing more. This was the final dragon's curse: a sickness of greed that turns those who should be allies into foes.
Over that cursed necklace, blood was nearly shed that day. Truly, it may have come to blood thereafter, had not the dragon come and scattered the dwarves far from Erebor.
And then the dragon came. Fire and ruin did Smaug rain on Dale and Erebor, for he had set his heart upon the riches under the mountain.
Again we fled the dragons' wrath and this time came to Erebor, the Lonely Mountain. But the great Scatha, wakened, wandered far and wide, troubling all.

Some may say I am cautious or old and weary, but still I say: let us dream no more dreams that may bring ruin on Durin's Folk. Let dragons sleep, and dwarves toil fruitfully where they dwell, and the work of our hands suffice.

'O reaches rich with gem and ore! Resplendent runes writ on the door! O kingly crown of ruby wrought! The forge-fires flaming ever-hot!'

'The Fast’s foundation stones were rent The throng spilled forth without relent Till Grár descended, stern and swift And broke the roof above the rift Grár the Grim-brow died for Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'

'Awake, again! What is this? I hear you, Etterfang! My sister is in battle, in pain! Rragh! I cannot reach her, my lair is sealed by fallen stone. Rend with all my fury, I still cannot carve an exit fast enough. Oh sister, sister, burn them all!'
'The harps sing loud, the fires burn low Our thoughts now stray to long ago When in the north and far away The anvils rang ‘neath Mountains Grey'

'Sister missing, dragon-whelps slain... I have known only sorrow in these grey peaks. Let sorrow take wing. I am fury, I am vengeance, I am Smaug the Golden, mighty and merciless. I will roam until I find dwarves - and then let them cower before my wrath!'

'Farin, Blackmattock, fared afar By shining sun and sheen of star And found what once was merely myth That red-veined peak, the Rusted Lith And stayed among the Hills of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold.'

'The war is lost, Thangorodrim broken, the glorious hosts fled. Sister Etterfang and I are the last of our proud line. But it is not over. Oh, no, for we will bring such terrible vengeance upon them... upon them all!'

'The wealth of Khazad-dûm is known Fair gems and mithril deck its throne And yet that gold-rich kingdom lacks The heart of hauberk, sword, and axe And so we went forth seeking Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'There is no sign of Sister Etterfang. Men here worship a dragon they name Draigoch. How amusing. Perhaps I will find my own clan of followers, though I so prefer to toy with them and then eat them.'
'In olden days, when all was sundered Our sires left strongholds wrecked and plundered And hewed new homes far under stone To carve a kingdom of their own'

'Lord Frár took up his liege’s maul He called his council, wise dwarves all To bid them bar his father’s grave So no fiend could escape the cave The crack was bound with bonds of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'Dwarves! How busily the noisy little insects carve up my peak, stealing my rightful wealth! They will see how Smaug the Golden welcomes intruders.'

'For years in Járnfast all was well But ages end, and times grow fell Black Thangorodrim fell in thunder And split the world’s stone spine asunder Shattered was the Hold of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'The harps grow still, the embers dim Our ballads glad grow black and grim For in the north and far away Our days drew short ‘neath Mountains Grey'

'Sister Etterfang is not in her lair. There was a struggle. I see the sheared stone from her thrashing claws, the ground scorched by her breath. The smell of a dwarf! She is still alive, I feel it. I will find you, sister.'

'What disturbs my slumber now? Rumbling. Am I trapped again? Grragh! What is this? The heads of five dragon-whelps, left before my cave... dwarf-axes sunk into them? Now, now at last, they have truly wakened Smaug's wrath!'

'His delvings found a wealth of ore Its worth a hundred hoards and more A carven keep he wrought to last Hewn from hillside: stout Járnfast Blackmattock became Lord of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'Now heed and hearken as I speak Of times that turned from blithe to bleak Fast and fearful came the fall Of fair, forlorn Thafar-gathol'

'We will bide our time high up in these mountains. This is a home for dragons. We will feast and gather treasure and grow strong. We will learn to cover where we are soft. But for now, sleep, and dreams of our revenge.'
Beryl, bloodstone, sapphire, sard Darkest onyx, diamond hard Gold and garnet filled their hoards And shone upon their shimm’ring swords'

Alas, the peril had not passed Morgoth's moaning host amassed In cracks and cleavings under hill Nameless beasts, with yearnings ill Fell things moved ’neath seams of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'

'Above the Pit, three gates of steel Upon the last, a mithril seal Graven rune-spells guard that curtain Break them not, or doom is certain Thus is writ the Rede of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'Ah, but how industrious these dwarves were while I slumbered! Carven halls of stone, gold and gemstones shaped and shined. It is worthy of my splendor, this new lair.'

'Still through long years of dauntless toil Lord Grár the Grave dug stone and soil The Fast was mended, whole once more And grander even than before And so returned our wealth of Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'Yet tales they tell of greater treasure Matchless wealth past mind and measure Mighty mithril, blazing bright That drenched the darkened depths with light'
'The Orcs whisper of a great dragon in the Misty Mountains. Perhaps it is Etterfang. I am loath to leave my hoard unguarded, but I must find her. It is good to stretch my wings and soar.'
'With iron fists and hammers strong They ruled a realm of storied song The glitt’ring mines and glimm’ring hall Of peerless, proud Thafar-gathol'

'The cleft collapsed; Grár was no more His mattock fell upon the floor Morgoth’s monsters shrieked and spit Imprisoned in the Howling Pit The horde remains entombed in Iron
Iron hard and iron cold'
'Awakened! Disturbed by little pests, scraping in the walls of my mountain. I can smell them, but I do not know the smell. It is not Men, no, nor Elves, nor Orcs…'

'And it was then you learned that Hrímil had devoured the Ring of Power, Tínya, along with the King of the Zhélruka who bore it. Diminished as you were, my lord, I have still not forgotten your fury.'
'And so Thorog served, if but for a moment, and now the Gaunt-lords are banished and Thorog returned to death. You are defeated, Lord Sauron, and the hated Hrímil flies free... but not for long.'

'You were still weakened, Lord Sauron, and when your feigned kindness did not avail you, you thought instead to bend Hrímil to your will. How fortunate you were then that Durin would soon slay her brother, Thorog the Mighty, at Helegrod....'

'In the depths of Dol Guldur, you essayed to wield your craft-skill anew. You forged a massive chain and etched it with runes of fell magic. For such brazenness, Hrímil would not be your servant... she was to be your prisoner.'

'You see, my lord, I will succeed where you have failed. I will turn the children of Hrímil against her, and she will serve me alone! Hrímil once said that you were a pretender, Lord Sauron. I think now she was right.'

'You spoke of a survivor of the Elder Days, a great Cold-dragon: Hrímil Frost-heart. Terrible in size and might, Hrímil had slain the Longbeards of the Steel Keep and now slumbered atop their hoards. It was she you desired above all.'

'Once again I returned to the halls of the Steel Keep, and once again Hrímil denied you. The loss of Thorog wounded her greatly, but her will remained unbroken. It was then Hrímil swore that she would never serve you, Lord Sauron.'

'Upon your return to Mordor, Barad-dûr rose anew and the Gaunt-lords crept out of the shadows of the Elder Days. One among them, Drugoth the Black, wielded the powers of necromancy, and it was then you devised your final vengeance against Hrímil Ring-eater.'

'At your bidding, the Gaunt-lords laboured to draw a powerful fell spirit into this realm. It was to be drawn to Helegrod where rested the remains of Hrímil's brother, Thorog the Mighty. Where Hrímil had resisted, Thorog would now serve in death.'

'In the halls of the Steel Keep, I learned that Hrímil had remained faithful to your master of old: the Dark Lord, Morgoth. Though you had claimed his title, she thought you a pretender... a failed servant who had imagined for himself some greater purpose.'

'Lord Sauron, what a legacy you have left behind! Your servants quarrel and seek in vain for dominion of Mordor, and the would-be Free Peoples pour through the Morannon to pick at your bones. If not for me, your grip on this realm would have slipped long ago.'

'It was not your loss of the Ring that unmade you, nor the armies of Men, but your pride and pettiness. Ah, but I sensed that weakness long ago... when you hid in frailty beneath Dol Guldur, desperate to wield the dragons that lingered in this realm.'

'Heedless of all peril, Hrímil had fallen into a deep slumber atop the hoards of the Steel Keep. Bound by your chains, Hrímil rose in sudden agony, shrieking as if she were consumed by unseen flame. Though she had devoured the Ring, Tínya still answered to its true master: Hrímil was yours at last.'

'It would be many years before you shed the guise of the Necromancer, and so I imprisoned Hrímil beneath the razed remains of Barad-dûr to await your return. There, she endured countless tortures, but never did she surrender the Ring.'

Zhélruka and Longbeard warriors alike adventured throughout Ered Mithrin for thousands of years, and the mountains still ring with the sound of their triumphs.
‘Thirteen kings, you say? Ah, it is an ill-omened number. How many more dwarves will die in sight of the Anvil before the dragons are swept away?’ – Kópat of the Zhélruka

Vethúg concealed herself in a high cavern behind a mighty waterfall near the Steel Keep, and waited. As Dáin raised his axe before his cheering people, she burst from her cave, the waterfall freezing and shattering into shards around her, and swept down upon the Longbeards.

The dragons lay sleeping in their hiding-places for hundreds of years, unremembered by their foes, but when they awoke they had not forgotten their ancient hatreds. So began the War of Dwarves and Dragons.

King Ilkún's search lasted for ten years, but ended in horror. While digging beneath the Anvil, the Zhélruka caused a great crack to split the glacier in twain. The cold-drakes who dwelt within Winterstith awoke and emerged from the rent, overwhelming the dwarves.

In time, Rúrek V came to be known as Rúrek the Slaughterer, and during his reign the Zhélruka waged war upon dragonkind; but it was an imprecise war, and the dragons that would prove most dangerous to them survived.
Countless dwarves set forth from Thikil-gundu and other lesser keeps in Ered Mithrin, eager to discover lost Thafar-gathol and seize its riches for their own. This eagerness proved their undoing.
Ingór charged the dragon, his sword held high, but he never landed a blow. Hrímil Frost-heart swallowed him entire: sword, armour, and all. Only the memory of that mighty warrior remains.
‘Longbeards hurry to battle. We Zhélruka must exercise restraint, if we can. Victory comes more slowly than defeat; treasure one and not the other.’ - Brátek IV, the Brash

The most prominent peaks of the Ered Mithrin number four: Wrathhorn, Undarbród, Thrumfall, and Winterstith. The Anvil at the base of this last has stood beyond memory of dwarves, and some say it will outstay them.

Old Mad Ubb, so quick and deft, Snatches, catches, leaves bereft The mothers of the babes he claims And leaves them crying out their names.
Caught a-thieving by his kin Cried cravenly to keep his skin Squawk and simper, squeal and sob, He fled a-howling from the mob
Somewhere yet he lurks and lingers, Scrabbling with his scabby fingers. ‘Neath forest dark or dusky hill Old Mad Ubb, he hungers still.
Keep close your sons and daughters dear Mind the moors and marshes drear For when the night grows black and cold Comes crawling Ubb the Mad and Old.
Now hear the lay of Old Mad Ubb Drowned his brother in the washing-tub Sunk his bones in the boggy pools Stole his silver, gold and jewels
For titbits tender still he yearns, With eyes that flare among the ferns: For foal and filly, kid and neat, And most of all, for children sweet.
They drove him deep into the bog Now he feasts on toad and frog Wriggling maggot, worm and grub: What a feast for Old Mad Ubb!
When cold wind wails and fir-tree creaks, Through the gloom of night he sneaks. O’er wooden wall and rooftops thatched, Unlocked window, gate unlatched.
In blackest shadows, his eyes burn Rav’ning hungry to return Lurking among ling and shrub: Weeping, creeping Old Mad Ubb.
So bolt your doors, make fast the shutters, And listen for his moans and mutters. Then light your lantern, torch, or lamp, To drive him back to dark and damp.

The passage of the mountains has never been easy, but with such noble companions it can be made less dangerous.

Woodmen and Beornings fought at the Battle of the Old Ford during the closing days of the War of the Ring. These pauldrons were worn bravely by one great warrior, but following the battle he set aside his weapons and vowed never to fight again. The Woodmen of Hultvís sent these pauldrons along to you, that they might still serve to protect those who need it.

Woodmen and Beornings fought at the Battle of the Old Ford during the closing days of the War of the Ring. One disgraced Woodman fled rather than fight, and he was slain by his fellows for cowardice.
